error_modes.label: ALTITUDE CONTROL THROUGH ENTRY AND RECOVERY

texts.0: SP, due to a late and coarse pitch input at the recovery, did not contain the altitude excursion of the maneuver and went more than 300 ft below the entry altitude. The aircraft was still descending with no reversal of the vertical trend when the IP took the controls to arrest the loss and re-establish level flight. SP did not reference the entry altitude at any point of the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to holding the nose low well past the cessation of the stall indications, allowed the aircraft to reach 300 ft below the entry altitude, exactly at the limit of the standard. The climb back to the entry altitude was started only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. SP did not use the altimeter trend to plan the level off, so the correction was late although no control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly delayed pitch reversal after the recovery, descended about 200 ft below the entry altitude, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. SP identified the excursion without any prompting and returned to the entry altitude within the following turn, arriving with a controlled rate and no overshoot above it. The subsequent stall was entered from the correct altitude.
texts.3: SP maintained the entry altitude before the stall and kept the total excursion of the maneuver within 150 ft of it. The vertical trend was reversed smoothly at the recovery and the aircraft was stabilized at the entry altitude with no overshoot. SP monitored the altimeter throughout the recovery and reported the altitude accurately.
texts.4: SP flew the entry altitude with excursions of a few tens of feet during the whole sequence of stalls, with the altimeter needle showing no perceptible overshoot at the level off. The pitch reversal was progressive and precisely timed, so the aircraft settled at the entry altitude at the first attempt each time.
texts.marginal: SP kept the altitude excursion inside the standard, but on every repetition the loss reached approximately 150 ft, consistently at the edge of the tight limit and always in the same low direction. The trend indicates that SP is trading altitude for a comfortable pitch attitude instead of controlling it. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch reversal earlier so that the excursion is reduced well inside the limit on the next sorties.

texts_at.0: SP flew the entry and recovery of the stall with the IP calling the point to reverse the pitch trend using the altimeter, due to first exposure to using an altimeter trend to plan a level off during a maneuver with a large pitch change. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to contain the altitude excursion independently on the next sortie, without the level off point being called.
texts_at.1: SP contained the total altitude excursion during entry and recovery to the level expected at this stage, with the excursion reaching about 280 feet below the entry altitude, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the altimeter trend not being used to plan the level off until late in the recovery. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to use the altimeter trend to plan the level off from the start of the recovery, not only late in it.
texts_at.2: SP identified the excursion without prompting and returned to the entry altitude within the following turn, arriving with a controlled rate and no overshoot, correcting an excursion of about 200 feet, due to a slightly delayed pitch reversal after the recovery. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to begin the pitch reversal the instant the stall is broken, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the entry altitude before the stall and kept the total excursion of the maneuver within about 110 feet, monitoring the altimeter throughout the recovery and reporting the altitude accurately, due to the vertical trend being reversed a shade later than ideal though smoothly and without overshoot. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reverse the vertical trend at the earliest possible point, not a shade later.

texts_above.1: SP contained the total altitude excursion during entry and recovery with the excursion reaching about 275 feet below the entry altitude, near the upper part of the tolerance, before the altimeter trend was used to plan and complete the level off. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a slightly delayed pitch reversal after the recovery, identified the excursion without prompting and returned to the entry altitude within the following turn, arriving with a controlled rate and no overshoot, the excursion held to about 200 feet. Beginning the pitch reversal the instant the stall is broken, rather than a beat after, would remove the correction from the recovery. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control through the stall sequence.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the entry altitude before the stall and kept the total excursion of the maneuver within about 110 feet, the vertical trend reversed smoothly at the recovery, the aircraft stabilized at the entry altitude with no overshoot while the altimeter was monitored throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude control through the stall sequence.
texts_above.4: SP flew the entry altitude with excursions of a few tens of feet during the whole sequence of stalls, the altimeter needle showing no perceptible overshoot at the level off, the pitch reversal progressive and precisely timed so the aircraft settled at the entry altitude at the first attempt each time. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control through the stall sequence.

error_modes.label: AIRSPEED CONTROL AT ENTRY AND AFTER RECOVERY

texts.0: SP, due to an uncontrolled power and pitch combination after the recovery, allowed the airspeed to diverge by more than 20 kts from the value required for the maneuver. The aircraft was accelerating towards the maneuvering limit with the nose still below the horizon when the IP intervened on the controls and on the power lever to re-establish the required airspeed. SP did not call any airspeed during the sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the power lever untouched while the nose was lowered at the recovery, let the airspeed deviate by 20 kts from the required value, at the limit of the standard. The power and pitch correction was applied only after the IP prompted verbally with the target airspeed. The deviation was arrested without any control input by the IP, but the aircraft remained off speed for a prolonged part of the recovery.
texts.2: SP, due to a small delay in coordinating power with the pitch change, allowed the airspeed to deviate by about 15 kts from the required value, between the 10 kts and 20 kts limits. SP detected the deviation on the airspeed indicator without prompting and corrected it promptly with a smooth power adjustment. The airspeed was stable at the required value before the next entry.
texts.3: SP set and maintained the entry airspeed and kept the deviation within 10 kts throughout the entry, the recovery and the level off. Power was coordinated with every pitch change, so the airspeed built up progressively with no overshoot of the target value. SP announced the airspeed at the recovery.
texts.4: SP controlled the airspeed with deviations of only a few knots across all repetitions, holding the entry value steady before each stall and rebuilding it without any overshoot after each recovery. The power lever movements were small and anticipatory rather than corrective.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the airspeed standard, but the deviations repeatedly approached 10 kts and were always corrected after the fact rather than anticipated. The pattern shows that SP is reacting to the airspeed indicator instead of leading it with power. SP is expected to coordinate power with pitch earlier so that the deviations stay clearly inside the tight limit.

texts_at.0: SP controlled airspeed at entry and after recovery with the IP calling the power adjustment needed to coordinate with the pitch change, due to first exposure to coordinating power with a pitch change during a stall recovery. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to control airspeed at entry and after recovery independently on the next sortie, without the power adjustment being called.
texts_at.1: SP controlled airspeed at entry and after recovery to the level expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 19 knots, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to power not being coordinated with the pitch change at the recovery until several seconds after it began. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to coordinate power with the pitch change from the first instant of the recovery, not several seconds after.
texts_at.2: SP detected the deviation on the airspeed indicator without prompting and corrected it promptly with a smooth power adjustment, correcting a deviation of about 15 knots, due to a small delay in coordinating power with the pitch change. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to size the power adjustment to the pitch change at the same instant, not with a small delay.
texts_at.3: SP set and maintained the entry airspeed and kept the deviation within about 8 knots throughout the entry, the recovery and the level off, power coordinated with every pitch change so airspeed built up progressively with no overshoot of the target, due to one power adjustment being a shade behind the pitch change though the airspeed still built progressively. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep every power adjustment exactly with the pitch change, not a shade behind it.

texts_above.1: SP controlled airspeed at entry and after recovery with the deviation reaching about 18 knots before power was coordinated with the pitch change and the required airspeed recovered. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP detected an airspeed deviation of about 15 knots on the indicator, caused by a small delay in coordinating power with the pitch change, and corrected it promptly with a smooth power adjustment, without prompting. Sizing the power adjustment to the pitch change at the same instant, rather than with a small delay, would remove the deviation before it develops. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound airspeed control through the stall sequence.
texts_above.3: SP set and maintained the entry airspeed and kept the deviation within about 8 knots throughout the entry, the recovery and the level off, power coordinated with every pitch change so airspeed built up progressively with no overshoot of the target value, the airspeed announced at the recovery. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed airspeed technique through the stall sequence.
texts_above.4: SP controlled airspeed with deviations of only a few knots across all repetitions, holding the entry value steady before each stall and rebuilding it without any overshoot after each recovery, the power lever movements small and anticipatory rather than corrective. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional airspeed control through the stall sequence.

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the pitch attitude, did not counter the yaw at the stall and exited more than 10 degrees off the entry heading. The aircraft continued to diverge in heading with rudder still misapplied until the IP took the controls to stop the yaw and return to the briefed heading. SP did not identify the direction of the divergence when asked.
texts.1: SP, due to an absent cross-check of the heading indicator during the recovery, exited 10 degrees off the entry heading, at the limit of the standard. The heading was regained only after the IP called the deviation and the direction of correction. SP kept the wings level thereafter, but the correction back to the entry heading was delayed and consumed most of the following straight leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief lapse in the cross-check while the power was being set, exited about 7 degrees off the entry heading, between the 5 and 10 degree limits. SP noticed the deviation on the heading indicator without prompting and corrected it with coordinated rudder and aileron before the next entry. The wings were kept level throughout the recovery.
texts.3: SP kept the yaw under control with timely rudder at the stall and exited within 5 degrees of the entry heading on each repetition. The heading indicator was included in the cross-check during the recovery and the exit heading was announced correctly. Aileron use remained coordinated with rudder.
texts.4: SP exited the maneuver on the entry heading with only a few degrees of deviation every time, holding the ball centred through the stall and the recovery. The rudder input matched the yaw tendency exactly, so no heading correction was needed after the recovery.
texts.marginal: SP held the exit heading inside the standard, but the deviation reached about 5 degrees on each repetition and always in the same direction, indicating an incomplete rudder input against the yaw at the stall. The cross-check of the heading indicator resumes only after the recovery is complete. SP is expected to include the heading in the cross-check during the recovery so that the exit deviation is reduced.

texts_at.0: SP controlled the exit heading with the IP calling for the heading indicator to be brought into the cross-check as the stall was entered, due to first exposure to including a heading reference in the cross-check through an entry dominated by pitch and AOA. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to control the exit heading independently on the next sortie, without the heading indicator being called.
texts_at.1: SP controlled the exit heading to the level expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 9 degrees, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the heading indicator being brought into the cross-check a beat later in the recovery than the yaw at the stall actually required. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to include the heading indicator in the cross-check from the moment the stall is entered, not only later in the recovery.
texts_at.2: SP noticed the deviation on the heading indicator without prompting and corrected it with coordinated rudder and aileron before the next entry, correcting a deviation of about 7 degrees, due to a brief lapse in the cross-check while power was being set. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the heading indicator in the cross-check through the power setting itself, not lapse during it.
texts_at.3: SP kept the yaw under control with timely rudder at the stall and exited within about 4 degrees of the entry heading on each repetition, the heading indicator included in the cross-check during the recovery and the exit heading announced correctly, due to one rudder input being a shade lighter than the yaw called for though the exit stayed well inside tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to match rudder pressure exactly to the yaw on every repetition, not slightly lighter.

texts_above.1: SP controlled the exit heading with the deviation reaching about 8 degrees before coordinated rudder and aileron corrected it against the heading indicator. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP noticed a deviation of about 7 degrees on the heading indicator, caused by a brief lapse in the cross-check while power was being set, and corrected it with coordinated rudder and aileron before the next entry, without prompting. Holding the heading indicator in the cross-check through the power setting itself, rather than lapsing during it, would remove the correction from the sequence. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid exit-heading control through the stall sequence.
texts_above.3: SP kept the yaw under control with timely rudder at the stall and exited within about 4 degrees of the entry heading on each repetition, the heading indicator included in the cross-check during the recovery and the exit heading announced correctly, aileron use remaining coordinated with rudder. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed exit-heading control through the stall sequence.
texts_above.4: SP exited the maneuver on the entry heading with only a few degrees of deviation every time, holding the ball centred through the stall and the recovery, the rudder input matching the yaw tendency exactly so no heading correction was needed after the recovery. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding exit-heading control through the stall sequence.

error_modes.label: CLIMB ATTITUDE AND BANK BEFORE THE STALL

texts.0: SP, due to an unstable pitch input during the deceleration, did not maintain the climb attitude before the stall and let the bank wander through and beyond the required value. The aircraft reached the stall in an attitude and bank that did not correspond to the exercise and the IP took the controls to prevent an uncontrolled roll at the buffet. The entry produced excursions beyond 300 ft in altitude and more than 20 kts in airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch rate that did not match the deceleration, held the climb attitude only intermittently and allowed the bank to reach the limit of the required value before the stall. SP set the attitude and the bank correctly only after repeated verbal indications by the IP. No control input by the IP was needed, but the aircraft entered the stall with parameters at the edge of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly aggressive initial pitch input, established the climb attitude with a small overshoot and let the bank vary moderately during the deceleration. SP detected the drift in attitude and bank on the attitude indicator and corrected it before the buffet, keeping the entry inside the tight limits of altitude and airspeed. The stall was entered with the intended attitude.
texts.3: SP established and maintained the climb attitude before the stall and held the required bank steady through the deceleration. The pitch rate matched the airspeed reduction, so the aircraft arrived at the buffet with the attitude and bank called in the briefing. The parameters of the entry remained inside the tight limits.
texts.4: SP set the climb attitude in one smooth movement and held it with negligible variation through the deceleration, with the bank fixed at the required value and the ball centred. The stall developed exactly in the attitude briefed, without any corrective input during the entry.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the climb attitude and the bank within the standards, but both required continuous small corrections and the bank drifted repeatedly towards the outer edge of the required value. The entry is being flown by correction rather than by a stable attitude reference. SP is expected to set the attitude and the bank once and hold them through the deceleration on the following sorties.

texts_at.0: SP established the climb attitude and held the required bank before the stall with the IP calling the pitch rate needed to match the deceleration, due to first exposure to matching a pitch rate to a deceleration continuously through an entry. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to establish the climb attitude and bank independently on the next sortie, without the pitch rate being called.
texts_at.1: SP established the climb attitude and held the required bank before the stall to the level expected at this stage, with altitude reaching about 280 feet and airspeed about 19 knots during the entry, near the upper part of both tolerances, due to the pitch rate not quite matching the deceleration through part of the entry. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to match the pitch rate to the deceleration continuously through the entry, not only for part of it.
texts_at.2: SP detected the drift in attitude and bank on the attitude indicator and corrected it before the buffet, keeping the entry inside the tight limits, correcting altitude of about 200 feet and airspeed of about 15 knots, due to a slightly aggressive initial pitch input that produced a small overshoot in the climb attitude. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to size the initial pitch input to avoid the overshoot, not correct it once established.
texts_at.3: SP established and maintained the climb attitude before the stall and held the required bank steady through the deceleration, the pitch rate matched the airspeed reduction so the aircraft arrived at the buffet with the attitude and bank called in the briefing, entry parameters held within about 110 feet and 8 knots, due to one small bank correction being applied a beat after it was needed rather than continuously. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the bank continuously through the deceleration, not correct it a beat after.

texts_above.1: SP established the climb attitude and held the required bank before the stall with altitude reaching about 275 feet and airspeed about 18 knots during the entry, both near the upper part of the tolerance, before the drift in attitude and bank was corrected before the buffet. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP detected a small overshoot in climb attitude and bank on the attitude indicator caused by a slightly aggressive initial pitch input, corrected it before the buffet and kept the entry inside the tight limits, altitude held to about 200 feet and airspeed to about 15 knots. Sizing the initial pitch input to avoid the overshoot, rather than correcting it once established, would remove the correction from the entry. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady climb-attitude and bank control before the stall.
texts_above.3: SP established and maintained the climb attitude before the stall and held the required bank steady through the deceleration, the pitch rate matching the airspeed reduction so the aircraft arrived at the buffet with the attitude and bank called in the briefing, entry parameters held within about 110 feet and 8 knots. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate climb-attitude and bank control.
texts_above.4: SP set the climb attitude in one smooth movement and held it with negligible variation through the deceleration, the bank fixed at the required value and the ball centred, the stall developing exactly in the attitude briefed with no corrective input during the entry. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary climb-attitude and bank control.

error_modes.label: MANEUVER EXECUTION PER TECHNIQUES AND PROCEDURES MANUAL

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient study of the maneuver, did not execute the Power on / ELP Stalls in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, omitting steps of the sequence and setting the power out of order. The maneuver was flown outside the described profile and the IP took the controls and terminated the exercise. SP could not state the correct sequence when debriefed in the air.
texts.1: SP, due to an imprecise recall of the sequence, executed the maneuver with steps taken out of the order described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. SP performed the correct sequence only after the IP verbally called each step. The maneuver was completed without any control input by the IP, but the parameters reached the limits of the standard because of the delay.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation at the transition from the entry to the recovery, executed one step of the sequence later than described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. SP recognized the omission without prompting and completed the sequence in the correct order, keeping the maneuver inside the standard. The remaining repetitions followed the described profile.
texts.3: SP executed the Power on / ELP Stalls in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with each step of the entry, the stall and the recovery taken in the described order and at the described point. The clearing turns and the configuration checks preceded the entry. SP verbalized the sequence accurately while flying it.
texts.4: SP executed the maneuver exactly as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual on every repetition, with the steps flowing without hesitation and without any dead time between the recovery and the setup for the next entry. The verbalization matched the actions precisely.
texts.marginal: SP executed the maneuver in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, but each step required a visible pause for recall before it was applied. The sequence is being reconstructed in flight rather than being known. SP is expected to consolidate the sequence on the ground so that the execution becomes continuous in the following sorties.

texts_at.0: SP executed the Power on / ELP Stalls sequence with the IP calling each step in the order described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, due to first exposure to recalling a multi-step sequence under the workload of the entry and recovery. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to execute the sequence independently on the next sortie, without each step being called.
texts_at.1: SP executed the Power on / ELP Stalls in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual to the level expected at this stage, with every step of the sequence flown, due to the transition from the entry to the recovery being hesitated on before the sequence continued in the described order. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to move from entry to recovery without a hesitation at the transition, not pause before continuing.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the omission without prompting and completed the sequence in the correct order, keeping the maneuver inside the standard, due to hesitation at the transition from the entry to the recovery that delayed one step of the sequence. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to remove the hesitation at the transition itself, not recognize and correct it afterward.
texts_at.3: SP executed the Power on / ELP Stalls in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with each step of the entry, the stall and the recovery taken in the described order and at the described point, the clearing turns and configuration checks preceding the entry, due to the sequence being verbalized a beat behind the actions rather than with them. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to verbalize the sequence in step with the actions, not a beat behind them.

texts_above.1: SP executed the Power on / ELP Stalls sequence, with one step taken later than described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual before the omission was recognized and the sequence completed in the correct order. The recognition followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a hesitation at the transition from the entry to the recovery that had delayed one step of the sequence, completed the sequence in the correct order without prompting, keeping the maneuver inside the standard. Removing the hesitation at the transition itself, rather than recognizing and correcting it afterward, would remove the correction from the sequence. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable maneuver-execution discipline.
texts_above.3: SP executed the Power on / ELP Stalls in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with each step of the entry, the stall and the recovery taken in the described order and at the described point, the clearing turns and configuration checks preceding the entry, the sequence verbalized accurately while flying it. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good maneuver-execution discipline.
texts_above.4: SP executed the maneuver exactly as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual on every repetition, the steps flowing without hesitation and without any dead time between the recovery and the setup for the next entry, the verbalization matching the actions precisely. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior maneuver-execution discipline.

error_modes.label: RECOVERY INITIATION AT THE ONSET OF LOSS OF CONTROL

texts.0: SP, due to a startle response at the onset of the departure from controlled flight that displaced the memorized recovery sequence, did not initiate the recovery at the first indication of loss of aircraft control. The stall was allowed to develop with the stick still aft and the loss exceeded 300 ft before the IP took the controls and recovered the aircraft. SP made no independent recovery input.
texts.1: SP, due to surprise at the buffet, delayed the recovery beyond the first indication of loss of aircraft control and started it only after the IP called for it. The subsequent inputs followed the manual criteria and the aircraft was recovered without any control input by the IP, but the delay drove the altitude loss to 300 ft, at the limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief hesitation at the onset of the buffet, initiated the recovery slightly after the first indication of loss of aircraft control. SP applied the recovery criteria of the Techniques and Procedures Manual without any prompting and contained the altitude loss at about 200 ft, between the tight and the wide limit. The following entries were recovered on the first indication.
texts.3: SP initiated the recovery at the first indication of loss of aircraft control, applying the criteria of the Techniques and Procedures Manual without delay. The stall was broken immediately and the altitude loss stayed within 150 ft. SP identified and called the indication that triggered the recovery.
texts.4: SP recognized the onset of loss of aircraft control instantly on every repetition and initiated the recovery with the correct inputs in a single continuous action, with no hesitation between the indication and the response. The stall was broken with the minimum possible excursion in altitude and airspeed.
texts.marginal: SP initiated the recovery within the standard, but each time only after a short pause at the buffet, and the pause was consistent across all the repetitions. The recognition of the onset is still deliberate rather than automatic. SP is expected to reach an immediate and reflexive recovery initiation, so that the reaction is not dependent on conscious confirmation of the indication.

texts_at.0: SP initiated the recovery at the onset of loss of aircraft control with the IP calling for the recovery criteria to be applied at the first indication, due to first exposure to responding to a startle-inducing indication with a memorized action rather than a pause. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to initiate the recovery at the onset of loss of control independently on the next sortie, without the criteria being called.
texts_at.1: SP initiated the recovery at the onset of loss of aircraft control to the level expected at this stage, with the altitude loss reaching about 280 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to a short pause at the buffet before the recovery criteria were applied. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply the recovery criteria at the first indication, not after a short pause at the buffet.
texts_at.2: SP applied the recovery criteria of the Techniques and Procedures Manual without prompting and contained the altitude loss, correcting a loss of about 200 feet, due to a brief hesitation at the onset of the buffet before the recovery was initiated. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to remove the hesitation at the onset of the buffet, not initiate the recovery slightly after it.
texts_at.3: SP initiated the recovery at the first indication of loss of aircraft control, applying the criteria of the Techniques and Procedures Manual without delay, the stall broken immediately with the altitude loss held within about 110 feet, identifying and calling the indication that triggered the recovery, due to the call itself lagging the control input by a beat rather than being simultaneous with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the call in the same instant as the control input, not a beat behind it.

texts_above.1: SP initiated the recovery at the onset of loss of aircraft control with the altitude loss reaching about 275 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, before the recovery criteria were applied and the aircraft recovered. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a brief hesitation at the onset of the buffet before the recovery was initiated, applied the recovery criteria of the Techniques and Procedures Manual without prompting and contained the altitude loss to about 200 feet. Removing the hesitation at the onset of the buffet, rather than initiating the recovery slightly after it, would remove the correction from the sequence. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured recovery-initiation technique.
texts_above.3: SP initiated the recovery at the first indication of loss of aircraft control, applying the criteria of the Techniques and Procedures Manual without delay, the stall broken immediately with the altitude loss staying within about 110 feet, identifying and calling the indication that triggered the recovery. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise recovery-initiation technique.
texts_above.4: SP recognized the onset of loss of aircraft control instantly on every repetition and initiated the recovery with the correct inputs in a single continuous action, with no hesitation between the indication and the response, the stall broken with the minimum possible excursion in altitude and airspeed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate recovery-initiation technique.

error_modes.label: LEVEL OFF WITH MINIMUM ALTITUDE LOSS

texts.0: SP, due to holding the recovery attitude far longer than necessary after the stall was broken, did not level off with the minimum altitude loss possible and the descent continued past 300 ft below the entry altitude. The aircraft was still going down with the power not yet matched to the attitude when the IP took the controls to level it. SP did not recognize that the aircraft had stopped stalling.
texts.1: SP, due to a level off that was flown as a single late pull instead of a progressive recovery to the horizon, lost 300 ft in the process, at the limit of the standard. SP levelled the aircraft only after the IP called the altitude and the correction. The maneuver was completed without any control input by the IP, but the altitude loss was clearly more than the maneuver required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late start of the pitch reversal, levelled the aircraft with an altitude loss of about 200 ft, between the tight and the wide limit. SP recognized the excess without prompting and completed the level off smoothly with the power matched to the attitude. The following repetitions were levelled with a noticeably smaller loss.
texts.3: SP levelled the aircraft off with the minimum altitude loss possible for the maneuver, keeping the total loss within 150 ft. The pitch reversal was started as soon as the stall was broken and was progressive, with power set to support the level off. The aircraft was stabilized level at the target altitude.
texts.4: SP levelled the aircraft with an altitude loss reduced to the minimum the maneuver allows, blending the break of the stall directly into the level off without any intermediate descent. Pitch and power arrived at the level flight values simultaneously and the aircraft stabilized immediately.
texts.marginal: SP levelled the aircraft within the altitude standard, but the loss reached approximately 150 ft on each repetition because the pitch reversal is started only once the airspeed is comfortably high. The technique is safe but not yet economical in altitude. SP is expected to begin the level off as soon as the stall is broken so that the loss is reduced further.

texts_at.0: SP levelled off with the minimum altitude loss possible for the maneuver with the IP calling the point to start the pitch reversal as soon as the stall was broken, due to first exposure to beginning a level off at the exact moment the stall is broken rather than once airspeed has built. error_modes.label: MANEUVER COMPLETION, ESTABLISHING A POSITIVE CLIMB

SP did not check the altimeter for an increasing trend.
texts.1: SP, due to holding a fixed attitude while the airspeed built up, delayed the additional back pressure needed to establish the climb and the aircraft mushed until the altitude loss reached 300 ft, at the limit of the standard. A positive climb was attained only after the IP called for it. No control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a late increase of back pressure as the power and the airspeed came up, allowed the descent to continue to about 200 ft below the entry altitude before the altimeter showed an increasing trend. SP noticed the missing climb without prompting and added the back pressure needed to establish it. The following recoveries were terminated with a positive climb without delay.
texts.3: SP increased the back stick pressure progressively as power and airspeed built up and attained a positive climb with the total altitude loss kept within 150 ft. The maneuver was called complete only when the altimeter showed increasing altitude.
texts.4: SP blended the increase of back pressure with the acceleration so precisely that the descent was arrested almost immediately and the altimeter reversed into a climb with an altitude loss of a few tens of feet. Completion of the maneuver was called at the correct moment on every repetition.

error_modes.label: ELP STALL RECOVERY PICTURE, PROP ARC ON THE HORIZON

texts.0: SP, due to recovering the ELP stall by feel instead of putting the prop arc on the horizon, did not lower the pitch attitude to the approximately 8 deg nose-low picture. The airspeed stayed more than 20 kts below the 120 KIAS glide value with the stick shaker intermittently active, and the IP took the controls to lower the nose and regain the glide speed. SP used the prop arc reference at none of the three ELP stalls.
texts.1: SP, due to setting a pitch attitude above the prop arc picture, recovered the configured ELP stall with the airspeed about 20 kts below the 120 KIAS glide value, at the limit of the standard. The nose was lowered to the correct picture only after the IP called the reference. The glide speed was regained without any control input by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete initial pitch reduction at the ELP stall recovery, held the airspeed about 15 kts below the target glide value for a short period. SP recognized that the prop arc was still above the horizon, lowered the pitch to the correct picture without prompting and regained the glide speed before the next profile point. The clean recovery was flown with the half prop arc picture correctly set.
texts.3: SP recovered each ELP stall by lowering the pitch attitude to the required picture, half prop arc on the horizon clean and prop arc on the horizon when configured, and regained the target glide speed with the deviation kept within 10 kts. texts.4: SP set the prop arc picture immediately and identically at each of the three ELP stalls, regaining 125 KIAS clean and 120 KIAS configured with deviations of only a few knots and without any secondary pitch correction. error_modes.label: MAINTAINING THE TURN AND PROFILE GROUND TRACK IN ELP STALL RECOVERY

The aircraft finished the recovery more than 10 deg off the required track with the Low Key position no longer achievable, and the IP took the controls to re-establish the profile. SP referenced no ground feature during the recovery.

The turn was re-established only after the IP prompted for the ground track. The profile was regained without any control input by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a partial reduction of the bank at the pitch change, allowed the ground track to move about 7 deg from the required one during the ELP stall recovery. The remaining ELP stalls were recovered with the turn maintained throughout.

Pitch and bank are being flown in sequence rather than together. SP is expected to maintain the turn while setting the recovery picture so that the profile ground track is not disturbed.
